record.narrative: Initial exploration is broad but biologically prioritized. The first 12 registered hypotheses emphasize strong candidate biomarkers and subgroups with plausible direction: oncogenic pathway dependencies (BRAF V600E to BRAF, KRAS mutation to KRAS, EGFR amplification to EGFR, ERBB2 amplification to ERBB2), synthetic lethality candidates (SMARCA4 or ARID1A chromatin remodeling defects with SMARCA2 dependency), MSI-associated WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with NFE2L2 dependency, MYC amplification with USP7/proteostasis dependency, and histology effects on EGFR/KRAS dependencies. For MDM2 and RIT1, I test directional expectations in the opposite sign because dependency may be weaker, not stronger, when the downstream pathway is already activated or p53 is lost. The later proposals increase coverage of essential and transport/translation genes: MYC amplification for POLR2A and RPL11, RB1 loss for KIF18A mitotic dependency, BRCA2 loss for replication stress/helicase dependency with DHX9, PTEN loss for STAT3 inflammatory/signaling dependency, KRAS mutation as a negative upstream-RAF/RAF-paralog hypothesis for RIT1, and a neutral research marker for TMED10 to screen arbitrary assays. More negative dependency means stronger dependency; positive anticipated raw contrasts mean expected weaker negative dependency. All cells should have >20 observations using the reported variable frequencies. Initial status is unresolved pending evidence.

I selected the 12 highest-prior mechanistic comparisons for discovery. These include classic oncogenic-driver dependencies (BRAF V600E with BRAF; EGFR amplification with EGFR; ERBB2 amplification with ERBB2; KRAS mutation with KRAS), the most established synthetic-lethality candidates (SMARCA4 and ARID1A chromatin-remodeling losses with SMARCA2; MSI-high with WRN; KEAP1 loss with NFE2L2; TP53 loss with MDM2; MYC amplification with USP7), and two additional replication/mitotic vulnerability hypotheses (RB1 loss with KIF18A; BRCA2 loss with DHX9). The remaining registered comparisons are retained for later allocation, especially histology, MYC effects on transcription/translation genes, PTEN-loss STAT3, KRAS-mutant RIT1, and arbitrary assay screening. No validation is appropriate yet because no direct evidence is available.

The strongest and most defensible discovery results are the very large positive signed estimates for the SMARCA2 and WRN hypotheses. For H5, SMARCA4-loss cells show a signed difference of about +0.784 (95% CI +0.765 to +0.803), i.e. raw SMARCA2 dependency is much more negative in SMARCA4-loss cells. This is far above a 10% relative scale change and has a narrow interval, so I accept the association in this dataset. For H7, MSI-high cells show a signed difference of about +0.790 (95% CI +0.760 to +0.819), i.e. raw WRN dependency is much more negative in MSI-high cells; I accept that association as well. These are associations in the supplied data, not causal claims.

H8 is the most informative negative finding. The claim predicted stronger NFE2L2 dependency with KEAP1 loss, but the signed estimate is about -0.796 (95% CI -0.816 to -0.776), meaning the raw contrast is strongly positive: KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency than KEAP1-intact cells. The interval excludes both null and the original hypothesized direction, so I reject the original claim and register a reversed hypothesis instead. This could reflect biological biology or another confound, so the reversal should be evaluated rather than interpreted mechanistically immediately.

H2 is borderline but scientifically important: EGFR amplification shows a signed difference of +0.025 (95% CI -0.000 to +0.051), roughly at the 10% threshold if relative size is approximated using the outcome's absolute scale. The interval narrowly crosses zero, so it is suggestive but not conclusive; I keep it unresolved and request independent validation. H4, H9, H15, and H16 have positive signed estimates but point estimates below the approximate 10% threshold and intervals spanning zero; I keep them unresolved or deferred rather than rejecting outright, especially where the exposure groups are smaller or the biological hypothesis remains plausible.

The other null findings are treated as unsupported for the registered direction. H1, H3, H6, and H10 show small or opposite signed effects, with H6 and H8 having clearly opposite directions when intervals are decisive. Multiple comparisons were limited to 12 discovery tests; the accepted effects are so large that they are unlikely to be multiple-testing artifacts, whereas the borderline and moderate results require follow-up. I have proposed library-restricted robustness checks for the accepted synthetic-lethality claims and lineage-interaction refinements for driver dependencies, plus a formal reversal claim for KEAP1/NFE2L2.

The independent validation for H2 does not support accepting the EGFR-amplification claim at this stage. The discovery estimate was signed +0.025, corresponding to a raw contrast in which EGFR-amplified cells had about 0.025 units stronger dependency; that is near a 10% relative difference on the roughly 0.25 absolute dependency scale used here. However, the independent validation estimate was smaller, signed +0.015 (independent 99.6% interval -0.025 to +0.056), and its interval spans both null and effects well below a 10% threshold. The discovery interval also barely excluded zero but included the null and included sub-threshold effects. Taken together, the evidence is suggestive of a small-to-moderate association, but it is not precise or consistent enough to conclude a scientifically/clinically meaningful 10% association in this dataset. I therefore leave H2 unresolved and active, with a better strategy being to ask whether the effect concentrates in adenocarcinoma or squamous subgroups rather than forcing an overall accept/reject decision.

The most important new conclusion is the reversal claim H20. H8 originally asked whether KEAP1 loss increases NFE2L2 dependency; it was strongly in the opposite direction. Re-expressed as H20 with the observed direction, the same discovery evidence gives a signed estimate of +0.796 (95% interval +0.776 to +0.816). That is a very large association: KEAP1-loss cells have substantially weaker NFE2L2 dependency than KEAP1-intact cells. Because the interval is extremely narrow relative to the effect and the magnitude is far above 10%, I accept H20 as a dataset association. This is a post-hoc reversal, so the claim should be framed as an observed association in this dataset and should not yet be interpreted as a general causal biological law.

The previously accepted claims H5 and H7 remain the strongest mechanistic dataset findings. SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency. These associations remain accepted but active because I have registered library-stratified robustness checks to assess whether they are robust across CRISPR library type rather than driven by screen technical structure. I also registered robustness checks for the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association and subgroup analyses for EGFR and KRAS driver dependencies. These next analyses are better allocated than further validation of H2 because H2's problem is precision and effect size, not merely independent sampling noise.

The central dataset findings so far are large associations: SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Before generalizing even within this dataset, I registered stratum-restricted robustness checks for each accepted association: male, adult, one named screen batch, and a higher-Cas9-activity subset. If these remain large, the conclusions are more stable to technical and sample-composition differences. If they attenuate, the conclusions should become conditional on the robust strata rather than global associations within this dataset.

I also added a specificity check for the SMARCA2 claim: among SMARCA4-intact cells, does ARID1A loss predict stronger SMARCA2 dependency? The overall ARID1A result was non-significant, so testing it within SMARCA4-intact cells helps distinguish ARID1A-independent vulnerability from confounding due to overlap with SMARCA4 loss. A null result would support specificity of the SMARCA4-loss effect; a positive result would suggest a broader chromatin-remodeling synthetic-lethality pattern.

The registered KRAS refinement tests KRAS-mutant dependency in STK11-loss cells, because KRAS co-mutations may create a more homogeneous biological context and increase effect precision. For untested MYC-amplification hypotheses on POLR2A and RPL11, I registered higher-growth-rate contexts where MYC-driven transcriptional and translational demand may be stronger. These are exploratory associations, not mechanism claims.

I also added subgroup refinements for previously null or weak findings where biological heterogeneity is plausible: ERBB2-amplification effects by histology, RB1-loss effects on KIF18A by histology, and TP53-loss effects on MDM2 within CDKN2A-intact cells. Finally, because the dataset includes constructed arbitrary markers D and E, I registered neutral-marker screens against TMED10 dependency. These help characterize the false-discovery or apparent-association background in this dataset without implying biological roles for those markers.

I selected 12 currently untested comparisons that address the highest-value scientific priorities from the discovery ledger. First, I requested library/QC robustness checks for the three large accepted associations. For SMARCA2 loss of SMARCA4, H23 and H24 test the effect within Avana screens and non-Avana screens; a persistent positive signed effect in both would make H5 less likely to be a single-library screen artifact. For WRN dependency, H25 tests MSI-high within Avana screens, and H43 tests MSI-high within higher-Cas9-activity screens, reducing reliance on the smallest subgroup while still probing technical robustness. For NFE2L2 dependency, H26 and H27 test the accepted reversed association, H20, in Avana and non-Avana screens; the signed positive direction means KEAP1-loss cells would again show weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Second, H39 tests biological specificity for SMARCA2 dependency by asking whether ARID1A loss predicts stronger SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-intact cells. This follows the rejected broad ARID1A result and can distinguish a SMARCA4-specific synthetic-lethality pattern from a broader chromatin-remodeling pattern. Third, I requested focused follow-up for borderline driver-dependency hypotheses: H21 tests whether EGFR-amplification effects are stronger in adenocarcinoma than squamous histology, and H48 tests whether KRAS-mutation effects on KRAS dependency are concentrated in STK11-loss cells, a plausible co-mutation context that may increase effect homogeneity. Finally, I requested new mechanistic coverage for outcomes with no direct evidence: H13 tests MYC amplification against POLR2A dependency, H17 tests PTEN loss against STAT3 dependency, and H18 tests KRAS mutation against RIT1 dependency in the opposite sign, i.e., whether KRAS mutation is associated with weaker RIT1 dependency. This allocation balances robustness of the strongest claims, specificity/co-mutation context, and broad discovery coverage while avoiding repeated already-tested comparisons.

The new discovery batch primarily tests robustness and specificity of the large accepted associations, plus several focused follow-ups. Using the same working convention that about 0.025 absolute dependency-score difference corresponds to a roughly 10% relative difference on the observed negative-scale dependency outcomes, the robustness results are decisive. For SMARCA2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger dependency both in Avana screens, H23/R14 estimate +0.781 (95% CI +0.760 to +0.802), and in non-Avana screens, H24/R15 estimate +0.801 (95% CI +0.748 to +0.853). These are far above the threshold and exclude null in the hypothesis direction, so I accept these stratum-specific robustness claims as supporting the global H5 association without suggesting it is confined to one CRISPR library. For WRN dependency, MSI-high is associated with much stronger dependency in Avana screens, H25/R16 +0.794 (95% CI +0.764 to +0.825), and in higher-Cas9-activity screens, H43/R17 +0.794 (95% CI +0.757 to +0.831), supporting H7. For the reversed NFE2L2 claim, KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency in both Avana screens, H26/R18 +0.796 (95% CI +0.774 to +0.818), and non-Avana screens, H27/R19 +0.794 (95% CI +0.746 to +0.842), supporting H20. I closed these individual robustness claims because the library/QC checks are sufficiently informative for the strata tested, while the global claims remain active for broader interpretation. H28 was deferred because the non-Avana MSI-high cell is expected to be too small for a valid discovery comparison.

H39 tests ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells. The signed estimate is essentially null, -0.003 (95% CI -0.025 to +0.019), opposite direction and below the threshold. I reject the registered ARID1A-specific claim. This does not prove biological specificity, but it is consistent with the global ARID1A null and supports the interpretation that the very large SMARCA2 association is primarily aligned with SMARCA4 loss rather than broader chromatin-remodeling losses in this dataset.

The driver/co-mutation follow-ups are more inconclusive. H21 tests whether EGFR-amplification effects on EGFR dependency are stronger in adenocarcinoma than squamous histology. The interaction estimate is small and in the opposite signed direction, -0.018 (95% CI -0.077 to +0.040), and the interval includes null and subthreshold effects in both directions. I leave it unresolved and active because direct subgroup estimates H29/H30 remain available and could clarify whether any overall weak signal concentrates by histology.

H48 tests KRAS dependency in STK11-loss cells. The signed estimate is +0.031 (95% CI -0.010 to +0.073), above the approximate 10% threshold at the point estimate, but the interval crosses zero and includes effects below threshold. This is biologically plausible co-mutation context but not conclusive. I leave H48 unresolved and active, and I request independent validation because validation is most useful here: the discovery point is promising but statistically and practically uncertain, whereas the largest accepted effects do not require validation before being recognized as dataset associations.

H17 is the strongest new mechanistic result. PTEN loss is associated with substantially stronger STAT3 dependency: signed estimate +0.267 (95% CI +0.215 to +0.319). In raw terms, PTEN-loss cells have a more negative STAT3 dependency score by about 0.215 to 0.319 units, far exceeding the approximate 10% threshold. I accept H17 as a dataset association, but not as a causal or externally generalizable claim. I mark it active and add robustness proposals because a large new association should be checked for technical or compositional confounding before overinterpreting.

H13 tests MYC amplification with POLR2A dependency. The estimate is tiny, +0.004 (95% CI -0.017 to +0.025), with the interval mostly below or at the threshold and crossing null. I reject the overall association, while the high-growth-rate refinement H49 can still address context-specific hypotheses. H18 tests whether KRAS mutation is associated with weaker RIT1 dependency. The estimate is negligible, +0.004 (95% CI -0.015 to +0.022), so I reject it. Overall, the new evidence strengthens robustness of the three accepted large effects, adds a large new PTEN/STAT3 dataset association, and identifies KRAS/STK11 as the main borderline claim worth independent validation.

The new independent validation for H48 is suggestive but not decisive. The discovery comparison within STK11-loss cells gave a signed estimate of about +0.031 (95% CI -0.010 to +0.073), and the independent validation gave a larger signed estimate of about +0.043 (independent 99.6% CI -0.024 to +0.109). Both point estimates are in the hypothesized direction—stronger KRAS dependency in KRAS-mutant cells relative to KRAS-wildtype cells within STK11-loss eligibility—and both exceed the approximate 0.025 absolute dependency-score scale that corresponds to a 10% relative difference on the observed negative-scale dependency outcomes. However, the intervals are wide, include null, include clinically subthreshold effects, and include at least some opposite-direction effect in the independent interval. Therefore, I do not accept H48 as evidence of a scientifically meaningful difference in this dataset. I keep it unresolved and active. The most plausible interpretation is that KRAS dependency may be enhanced in KRAS-mutant cells that have STK11 loss, but the subgroup sample and validation precision are insufficient for a confident conclusion. This remains an association claim, not a causal or externally generalizable mechanism. The next analyses should test whether the KRAS-mutation effect is genuinely concentrated in STK11-loss cells rather than being a broader KRAS-mutation effect diluted by small cell counts. I registered an interaction test comparing the KRAS-mutation effect in STK11-loss cells with the effect in STK11-intact cells, plus a direct complement estimate within STK11-intact cells. A positive interaction with a small or null complement effect would strengthen the case for context-specific KRAS/STK11 co-mutation biology in this dataset; a substantial complement effect would make H48 more consistent with a general KRAS-mutation association and would shift attention toward the overall KRAS claim and its precision. I also keep the STAT3/PTEN-loss robustness checks as high priority because PTEN loss showed a much larger accepted dataset association and still needs technical robustness assessment. H2 and H4 remain unresolved for similar precision/effect-size reasons rather than because of clear null evidence.

This exploratory batch is organized around three scientific priorities. First, the PTEN-loss/STAT3-dependency association (H17) is large and accepted but needs context and robustness assessment beyond the already-registered library/Cas9/lineage checks. I registered an interaction test asking whether PTEN loss concentrates STAT3 dependency more strongly in PIK3CA-mutant cells, which would suggest a coherent PI3K/PTEN-STAT3 axis, and a direct estimate in high IFN-gamma cells to test whether inflammatory signaling amplifies the PTEN-loss effect. Second, I added specificity and context checks for the three largest accepted associations: SMARCA4 loss effect among ARID1A-intact cells tests whether the SMARCA2 vulnerability depends on ARID1A co-loss; MSI-high WRN effect among higher mutation burden distinguishes MSI-high specificity from a general hypermutation proxy; KEAP1 loss effect among STK11-loss cells tests whether the reversed NFE2L2 association persists in a co-mutation context. Third, I broadened pathway hypotheses: BRAF V600E may weaken upstream RIT1 dependency because downstream MAPK activation reduces upstream node dependency; KRAS mutation may weaken EGFR dependency for the same reason. MYC amplification was null overall for POLR2A and RPL11, so I test high-MYC-expression contexts where MYC-driven transcriptional/translational demand should be most relevant. TP53 loss is tested against USP7 dependency because of their shared p53-pathway biology. Finally, I test the STK11-loss effect on KRAS dependency within KRAS-mutant cells as a reverse perspective to H48, which tested the KRAS-mutation effect within STK11-loss cells. All proposals are associations within this dataset, not causal claims.

I selected 12 untested analyses that combine robustness for the newly accepted PTEN/STAT3 association, resolution of the borderline KRAS/STK11 pattern, specificity checks for the large accepted associations, and a few broad mechanistic tests. H57 and H58 stratify PTEN-loss STAT3-dependency effect by CRISPR library. If the large H17 effect remains positive in both Avana and non-Avana screens, it is less likely to be a library artifact; attenuation in non-Avana would make the accepted association library-conditional within this dataset. H62 and H63 directly test the logic behind H48: H62 asks whether the KRAS-mutation effect on KRAS dependency is stronger in STK11-loss cells than in STK11-intact cells, while H63 estimates the complement effect in STK11-intact cells. Together with H48 and its validation, these can distinguish a context-specific co-mutation effect from a broader KRAS-mutation association diluted by subgroup size. H74 asks the reverse within KRAS-mutant cells: does STK11 loss itself associate with stronger KRAS dependency? H64 tests whether PTEN-loss effects on STAT3 are stronger in PIK3CA-mutant cells, probing a coherent PI3K/PTEN context. H66, H67, and H68 provide complementary specificity/context checks for the very large SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2 associations: SMARCA4-loss effect among ARID1A-intact cells, MSI-high effect among higher mutation-burden cells, and KEAP1-loss effect among STK11-loss cells. These help determine whether the large associations are robust within co-alteration contexts and not solely driven by overlap with nearby alterations. H69 and H70 are cross-pathway tests: BRAF V600E or KRAS mutation may reduce dependency on upstream nodes RIT1 or EGFR if downstream MAPK activation bypasses those upstream inputs. H73 tests USP7 dependency under TP53 loss, a p53-pathway-related hypothesis not previously examined for this outcome. I did not select high-MYC-expression POLR2A/RPL11 refinements this batch because MYC amplification was null overall and the pathway context is less mature than the selected robustness/co-mutation and MAPK checks.

These results mostly strengthen or contextualize the large accepted associations and add one new large mechanistic association, while leaving the KRAS/STK11 cluster uncertain. H57/R27 tests PTEN loss on STAT3 dependency within Avana screens: signed estimate +0.288 (95% CI +0.232 to +0.343), far above the approximate 0.025 absolute-scale threshold and excluding null in the hypothesis direction. I accept H57 and close it as a robustness stratum supporting H17. H58/R28 is the non-Avana complement: signed estimate +0.092 (95% CI -0.062 to +0.246), but only 27 exposed cells; it is promising in point estimate yet too imprecise to accept or reject. Thus the accepted PTEN/STAT3 association is robust in the major Avana stratum but library-conditional precision remains limited outside Avana.

The KRAS/STK11 follow-ups remain inconclusive. H62/R29 interaction estimate +0.022 (95% CI -0.024 to +0.067) is near the approximate clinical threshold in the expected direction but crosses null and includes both subthreshold and larger effects. H63/R30 complement KRAS-mutation effect in STK11-intact cells is small, +0.010 (95% CI -0.010 to +0.029), with only its upper end marginally approaching the threshold. H74/R38 reverse test, STK11 loss within KRAS-mutant cells, is +0.014 (95% CI -0.026 to +0.053). The pattern mildly favors a co-mutation-specific effect, but no individual comparison is decisive enough to accept a scientifically meaningful difference. I keep H62 and H74 active and defer H63.

H64/R31 is too imprecise for PIK3CA-mutant context because only 38 cells contribute to one exposed subgroup: interaction estimate +0.001 (95% CI -0.150 to +0.152). I leave it unresolved and deferred rather than reject or interpret the null point estimate.

The specificity/context checks for the three largest accepted effects are decisive. H66/R32 shows that SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency even among ARID1A-intact cells: +0.777 (95% CI +0.756 to +0.798). H67/R33 shows MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency even among higher mutation-burden cells: +0.780 (95% CI +0.749 to +0.811). H68/R34 shows KEAP1 loss predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency in the hypothesized direction even among STK11-loss cells: +0.775 (95% CI +0.727 to +0.823). These are far beyond the threshold, exclude null, and support that the global H5, H7, and H20 associations are not driven solely by the excluded co-alteration contexts. I accept and close each as informative robustness/context checks.

For the broad MAPK cross-pathway tests, H69/R35 tests BRAF V600E against weaker RIT1 dependency: signed estimate +0.004 (95% CI -0.025 to +0.033). The point estimate is negligible and the interval barely touches clinically meaningful positive values, so I leave it unresolved and defer. H70/R36 tests KRAS mutation against weaker EGFR dependency: signed estimate -0.010 (95% CI -0.027 to +0.008), opposite direction and below threshold; I reject it. H73/R37 is the strongest new discovery: TP53 loss in the hypothesized +1 direction gives +0.396 (95% CI +0.325 to +0.467). Because positive signed values correspond to higher, less negative USP7 dependency scores, this supports TP53-loss cells having weaker USP7 dependency relative to TP53-intact cells in this dataset. It is large, precise, and scientifically coherent with p53-pathway biology, but I treat it only as a dataset association. I accept H73, keep it active, and request independent validation because it is a new large association and validation would test whether it is reproducible outside this discovery partition rather than whether its discovery estimate is internally strong.

The newly delivered validations substantially strengthen two accepted dataset associations but do not resolve the EGFR-amplification claim. For H5, SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in the discovery estimate and is independently validated with a signed estimate of +0.786 and an independent interval approximately +0.757 to +0.815. This is far beyond the approximate clinical threshold proxy used for these negative-scale dependency outcomes and excludes null in the hypothesized direction. I therefore keep H5 accepted and active: the association is reproducible outside the discovery partition, although its external biological generality remains unproven. For H73, TP53 loss in the +1 direction corresponds to higher, less negative USP7 dependency scores, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency in TP53-loss cells. The discovery signed estimate was +0.396 (95% CI +0.325 to +0.467), and the independent validation signed estimate was +0.382 with an independent interval approximately +0.280 to +0.485. Validation preserves the effect size and excludes null in the hypothesized direction, so I accept H73 as a dataset association and keep it active for further context/robustness checks. This should not be interpreted as a causal USP7 mechanism; it is an association between measured TP53-loss status and a dependency-score phenotype in this dataset. H2 remains unresolved. The discovery estimate for EGFR amplification was only borderline, signed +0.025 with a 95% interval essentially touching null on one side, and the independent validation was weaker, signed +0.015 with an independent interval approximately -0.025 to +0.056. The validation point estimate is below the approximate clinically meaningful absolute threshold and the interval includes both subthreshold and opposite-direction effects. Thus I do not accept H2. I keep it unresolved and active because the histology-specific and interaction comparisons may still clarify whether any small EGFR-amplification effect is concentrated in adenocarcinoma or diluted across subtypes. The overall KRAS/STK11 cluster remains suggestive but unresolved, as does non-Avana PTEN/STAT3 precision. The next most informative work is to characterize robustness of the validated/large accepted associations across technical QC and histologic strata, especially the new TP53-loss/USP7 association, and to test whether KRAS dependency effects are further modulated by TP53 loss. These proposals are registered as refinements/robustness checks of existing accepted or unresolved associations, not as new claims about causality.

This exploratory batch balances follow-up of accepted large associations, clarification of unresolved co-mutation signals, and one new DNA-repair hypothesis. For USP7, TP53-loss is now independently associated with weaker dependency; I test MYC-amplified and CDKN2A-loss contexts to ask whether the p53-pathway association is general or modified by co-alterations in related proliferative/pathway programs. For EGFR amplification, discovery and validation were only suggestive, so I stratify by KRAS mutation: if the effect is concentrated in KRAS-wildtype cells, it may be biologically coherent but diluted by KRAS-mutant bypass; if KRAS-mutant cells show attenuation, that supports a pathway-specific interpretation. For PTEN-loss/STAT3 dependency, high hypoxia and STK11-loss contexts test whether inflammatory or immune-evasion/immune-co-mutation states amplify the accepted stronger STAT3 dependency. For KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 dependency, TP53-loss and MYC contexts test whether the reversed, weaker-dependency association persists in common co-altered lung cancer backgrounds. For SMARCA2, high mutation burden tests whether the very large SMARCA4-loss vulnerability is confounded by hypermutant states. For KRAS dependency, I refine the suggestive KRAS/STK11 cluster by estimating the KRAS-mutation effect among STK11-loss cells that remain TP53-intact, helping distinguish a co-mutation-specific effect from dilution across unrelated TP53-loss states. For WRN, low mutation burden complements the accepted high-burden check and tests whether MSI-high specificity survives in lower-burden backgrounds. Finally, BRCA2-loss is tested against WRN dependency as a new replication-stress/DNA-repair hypothesis. All proposed comparisons are observational dataset associations, not causal claims or externally generalizable mechanisms.

Selected the 12 most informative untested claims from the latest batch. H87-H88 test whether the newly validated TP53-loss/USP7 weaker-dependency association is modified by co-alterations in p53-pathway-adjacent or proliferation contexts (MYC amplification, CDKN2A loss). H89-H90 stratify the unresolved EGFR-amplification/EGFR-dependency signal by KRAS mutation, distinguishing possible bypass attenuation in KRAS-mutant cells from a clearer effect in KRAS-wildtype cells. H91-H92 probe whether PTEN-loss/stronger STAT3 dependency is amplified under hypoxic or STK11-loss co-mutation backgrounds. H93-H94 test whether KEAP1-loss/ weaker NFE2L2 dependency persists under TP53-loss or MYC-amplified backgrounds. H95 checks whether the very large SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2-dependency association is robust among higher mutation-burden cells rather than merely a hypermutation proxy. H96 refines the suggestive KRAS/STK11 cluster by estimating KRAS-mutation effect among STK11-loss, TP53-intact cells. H97 complements the accepted high-burden MSI-high/WRN check by testing low mutation burden. H98 introduces a new replication-stress/DNA-repair hypothesis: BRCA2 loss associated with stronger WRN dependency. These analyses are treated as dataset associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

The new batch strongly strengthens the existing large associations and gives informative co-alteration context checks, while leaving the EGFR and some KRAS subgroup questions borderline. H87 and H88 show that TP53 loss remains associated with weaker USP7 dependency in MYC-amplified cells (signed +0.510, 95% CI +0.345 to +0.674) and in CDKN2A-loss cells (signed +0.393, 95% CI +0.239 to +0.548); both are large, exclude null, and are accepted/closed as context strata for H73. H91 and H92 show PTEN loss remains associated with stronger STAT3 dependency under high hypoxia (signed +0.237, CI +0.134 to +0.340) and in STK11-loss cells (signed +0.258, CI +0.134 to +0.382); accepted/closed as robustness contexts for H17. H93 and H94 show KEAP1 loss remains associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency under TP53 loss (+0.810, CI +0.763 to +0.857) and MYC amplification (+0.790, CI +0.729 to +0.850); accepted/closed as robustness contexts for H20. H95 shows SMARCA4-loss association with stronger SMARCA2 dependency is robust among higher mutation-burden cells (+0.795, CI +0.768 to +0.821), supporting that it is not merely a hypermutation proxy; accepted/closed for H5. H96 is the key borderline positive: KRAS mutation is associated with stronger KRAS dependency among STK11-loss, TP53-intact cells (signed +0.052, CI +0.008 to +0.096; exposed n=88). The point exceeds the approximate threshold and the interval excludes null, and this refines the suggestive KRAS/STK11 cluster, so I accept it as a dataset association but keep it active and request independent validation because the lower interval bound is still below the approximate meaningful difference and the finding is subgroup-specific. EGFR amplification remains unresolved: in KRAS-wildtype cells H89 is weak (+0.016, CI -0.014 to +0.046), while in KRAS-mutant cells H90 is intriguing (+0.053, CI +0.004 to +0.103) but based on only 43 exposed cells and the overall H2 association is not accepted, so H90 remains unresolved active rather than accepted. H97 cannot be estimated because there are no MSI-high observations in the low-mutation-burden eligibility; this closes that impossible stratum without interpreting it as null. H98 gives a near-zero BRCA2-loss/WRN estimate (-0.00008, CI -0.045 to +0.045), so the directional hypothesis is unsupported but the interval is too wide to confidently exclude a small meaningful effect; deferred. All accepted statements remain dataset associations, not causal or generally validated biological mechanisms.

The newly delivered validations materially weaken the KRAS/STK11 subgroup cluster and do not support the refined KRAS-mutation effect among STK11-loss TP53-intact cells. For H48, the direct STK11-loss stratification is now assessed with both discovery and independent validation. Discovery gave signed +0.031 with a 95% interval crossing null, and independent validation gave signed +0.043 with an independent interval approximately -0.024 to +0.109. The point estimates favor stronger KRAS dependency in KRAS-mutant STK11-loss cells, and some of the interval range includes clinically meaningful differences under the approximate relative threshold, but the independent interval also includes null, opposite-direction effects, and clearly subthreshold values. Therefore H48 remains unresolved rather than accepted. Because the less-refined H48 estimate is not decisive and the refined H96 estimate failed validation, I defer H48 rather than keep it as a primary active claim, while leaving related KRAS co-mutation interactions in the investigation pool. H96 is explicitly reassessed and downgraded from provisional acceptance to unresolved and closed. Its discovery estimate was signed +0.052 with a borderline interval excluding null, but independent validation returned signed +0.017 with a wide interval approximately -0.058 to +0.092. The validation point estimate is below the approximate 10% relative significance proxy on the usual scale of these dependency outcomes and cannot confirm the subgroup-specific association. The most defensible conclusion is that the KRAS-mutation stronger-dependency signal in STK11-loss TP53-intact cells is not reproduced at a clinically meaningful or statistically decisive level in the supplied data. This does not alter the larger validated associations: H5 SMARCA4 loss associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency and H73 TP53 loss associated with weaker USP7 dependency remain accepted and validated. The other accepted associations H7 MSI-high associated with much stronger WRN dependency, H17 PTEN loss associated with stronger STAT3 dependency, and H20 KEAP1 loss associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency also remain accepted, though not all have independent validation. The failed KRAS refinement is a useful caution against overinterpreting borderline subgroup findings. Next investigation should focus on technical QC and histologic robustness of the validated large associations, EGFR conditional effects, and whether the KRAS co-mutation cluster is better explained by TP53-loss rather than TP53-intact STK11-loss subgroups.

I will prioritize three complementary kinds of comparisons. First, I register high-value robustness strata for the core accepted dataset associations. H5 and H73 are already independently validated, but H7 MSI-high/WRN, H17 PTEN-loss/STAT3, and H20 KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 are not; therefore additional strong and precise stratum estimates could motivate later validation. Serum context, proliferation rate, EMT phenotype, and lineage provide non-CRISPR technical/biological settings in which to ask whether the large accepted effects are stable or context-dependent. These are still dataset associations, not external validation. Second, I focus on unresolved receptor-tyrosine-kinase amplification questions. ERBB2 amplification is null overall in H3, but it may be histology-dependent; an interaction with adenocarcinoma versus squamous can test whether the direct H51/H52 subgroup analyses are masking a context-specific effect. For EGFR amplification, H89 is weak overall in KRAS-wildtype cells and H90 is underpowered but suggestive in KRAS-mutant cells; the proposed KRAS-wildtype/adenocarcinoma stratum is a biologically coherent condition in which EGFR amplification might confer stronger EGFR dependency without KRAS bypass. Third, I introduce new but plausible biological probes: MYC amplification and mitotic KIF18A dependency, TP53 loss and DHX9 replication-stress dependency, KRAS mutation and weaker BRAF dependency from pathway bypass, TP53 loss and MDM2 dependency among high MYC-expression cells where the p53-MDM2 axis may be most relevant, and BRCA2-loss/WRN dependency among MSI-negative cells to ask whether BRCA2 has an effect independent of the dominant MSI-high WRN signal. For these dependency outcomes, a 10% relative difference corresponds to roughly a mean score difference in the low hundredths to few tenths depending on the outcome mean; very large accepted effects are far above this, while smaller receptor-tyrosine-kinase or co-mutation effects will require tight confidence intervals before being accepted.

This batch selects 12 existing, currently untested comparisons that are most informative for both focused follow-up and broad exploration. First, I test robustness of accepted but not independently validated associations. H17 PTEN-loss -> stronger STAT3 dependency is currently supported by overall discovery R24 signed +0.267, 95% CI +0.215 to +0.319, and by accepted context strata under hypoxia and STK11 loss. H59 and H105 test whether this remains under adequate Cas9 activity and high EMT score, respectively; these are non-CRISPR technical/phenotypic robustness checks. H20 KEAP1-loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency is enormous in R8 signed +0.796, CI +0.776 to +0.816; H106 tests a high-serum culture context. H7 MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency is also very large in R7 signed +0.790, CI +0.760 to +0.819; H107 tests a high-serum context. H77 tests the accepted/validated H73 TP53-loss -> weaker USP7 dependency under high Cas9 activity, providing QC robustness for a validated association. Second, I prioritize clarification of the KRAS co-mutation signal. H86 estimates whether the KRAS mutation -> stronger KRAS dependency association differs by TP53 loss, with direction -1 already signed to the stronger-dependency hypothesis. Given the failed or imprecise validation of KRAS/STK11 refinements, this broad TP53-loss interaction is a conservative next step. Third, I test unresolved receptor-tyrosine-kinase amplification hypotheses that could be masked by overall null or underpowered subgroup estimates. H109 formally tests whether ERBB2 amplification effect on ERBB2 dependency differs between adenocarcinoma and squamous cells. H115 tests the biologically coherent KRAS-wildtype adenocarcinoma stratum for EGFR amplification, where bypass signaling is less likely. Fourth, I add plausible new probes: H111 MYC amplification -> stronger KIF18A dependency, H112 TP53 loss -> stronger DHX9 replication-stress dependency, H113 KRAS mutation -> weaker BRAF dependency via MAPK bypass, and H114 TP53 loss -> weaker MDM2 dependency among high MYC expression. Each analysis will return a Welch mean_difference or interaction estimate with a 95% discovery interval and cell counts. I will judge clinically meaningfulness against the approximate 10% relative threshold, noting that for dependency scores around -0.25 this corresponds to roughly a 0.025 mean-score shift, while accepted large associations are far above this. Small receptor-tyrosine-kinase or co-mutation effects will require tight intervals excluding subthreshold values before acceptance.

This batch delivers decisive robustness evidence for the accepted core dataset associations and several informative negative or inconclusive new probes. For H59, PTEN loss remains associated with much stronger STAT3 dependency under adequate Cas9 activity (signed estimate +0.224, 95% CI +0.159 to +0.289; exposed n=161). The effect is large, excludes null, and is far above the approximate 10% relative threshold for STAT3 dependency (roughly a 0.028 mean-score shift near the overall STAT3 mean), so it is accepted and closed as a QC robustness stratum for H17. H105 strengthens H17 further: in high-EMT cells, PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency (+0.378, CI +0.261 to +0.495; exposed n=58). Although the exposed cell is modest, the interval is tight enough and the effect is well above the approximate threshold; accepted and closed. H106 and H107 similarly confirm the KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 and MSI-high/WRN associations in a high-serum culture context: KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency is enormous (+0.814, CI +0.788 to +0.840), and MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency remains enormous (+0.784, CI +0.746 to +0.823). Both exclude null, are far above clinically meaningful thresholds for those outcomes, and are accepted as robustness strata and closed. H77 confirms that TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency even under adequate Cas9 activity (+0.426, CI +0.339 to +0.513), far above the approximate 0.018 threshold for USP7 dependency; accepted and closed. Because H17 now has strong overall and robustness evidence but lacks independent validation, I request independent validation of H17 rather than H7 or H20, whose effects are already extraordinarily precise. The new KRAS co-mutation interaction H86 is not supportive of the claimed TP53-loss-specific enhancement of KRAS dependency (signed interaction -0.018, CI -0.060 to +0.025). Given the failed and imprecise prior KRAS/STK11 refinements and the interval remaining compatible with only a small positive interaction, this is inconclusive but not worth further follow-up; I mark it unresolved and closed. H109 rejects the claimed adenocarcinoma-specific ERBB2 amplification effect: the interaction is negative (-0.051, CI -0.117 to +0.015), and the upper bound is below the approximate 0.026 clinically meaningful threshold for ERBB2 dependency, so a scientifically meaningful adenocarcinoma-enhanced ERBB2 dependency is not supported. H112 rejects TP53 loss associated with stronger DHX9 dependency: the signed estimate is negative (-0.020, CI -0.039 to -0.001), indicating the opposite direction, though not a strongly meaningful reversed effect worth promoting now. H113 rejects KRAS mutation associated with weaker BRAF dependency (+0? signed -0.016, CI -0.034 to +0.001; claimed positive/upper below threshold). H111, H114, and H115 remain unresolved and deferred: each point estimate is below or near the approximate clinical threshold and the intervals are too broad or include null; further follow-up is possible but should not crowd out more robust core claims. All statements remain observational associations within this supplied dataset, not causal mechanisms or claims of external generalizability.

The newly delivered validation materially strengthens the current core evidence base. First, H17 is now independently validated: PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency with signed discovery estimate +0.267, 95% CI +0.215 to +0.319, and independent validation estimate +0.307, independent CI +0.228 to +0.387. Both exclude null and far exceed the approximate 10% relative threshold for STAT3 dependency (roughly +0.028 near the overall mean), so I accept H17 and close its direct investigation while retaining accepted context strata for robustness. Response-deadline claims H5 and H73 are also confirmed. H5 SMARCA4 loss remains associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in independent validation (+0.786, independent CI +0.757 to +0.815), consistent with discovery (+0.784, CI +0.765 to +0.803). H73 TP53 loss remains associated with weaker USP7 dependency (+0.382, independent CI +0.280 to +0.485), consistent with discovery (+0.396, CI +0.325 to +0.467). These are accepted, validated dataset associations; their investigation is closed because they are now sufficiently characterized and robust across several technical and co-alteration strata.

The current supported findings within this supplied dataset are: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency; PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency; TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency. All are observational associations among 2000 lung-cell-line profiles with measured predictors, not causal claims or generalizable biological mechanisms. More negative dependency scores mean stronger dependency; positive signed estimates indicate the claimed direction, including the NFE2L2 reversal where KEAP1 loss moves the score toward weaker dependency. H7 and H20 remain accepted without independent validation, but their discovery effects are extremely large and robust across CRISPR library, Cas9 QC, mutation burden, serum, and co-alteration contexts.

Negative or unsupported findings are also informative. BRAF V600E was not associated with stronger BRAF dependency; ERBB2 amplification was not associated with stronger ERBB2 dependency overall and did not show an adenocarcinoma-specific enhancement; MYC amplification was not associated with stronger POLR2A or USP7 dependency; KRAS mutation was not associated with weaker BRAF dependency, stronger RIT1 dependency, or weaker EGFR dependency; TP53 loss was not associated with stronger DHX9 dependency in the claimed direction. Overall EGFR amplification remains a negative/uncertain finding after independent validation: discovery was marginal (R2 +0.025, CI -0.000 to +0.051), validation did not reproduce a clinically meaningful effect (R13 +0.015, independent CI -0.025 to +0.056), so I close H2 as unresolved rather than accepted. Overall KRAS mutation associated with stronger KRAS dependency is also left unresolved and closed as not decisive: the point estimate is below the approximate 10% relative threshold and the interval includes subthreshold values (R4 +0.014, CI -0.004 to +0.031). The KRAS co-mutation subgroup cluster remains weakly supported at best and failed validation in prior refinements, so I am not promoting it further.

Unresolved uncertainty remains around EGFR amplification conditional on KRAS/lineage context, formal lineage heterogeneity for core accepted associations, research-marker associations with TMED10, MYC-related dependencies such as RPL11 and KIF18A, TP53-MDM2 contexts, and BRCA2-related DNA-repair dependencies. The most informative next analyses are independent validation of the two accepted but still non-validated core associations, prioritizing H20 KEAP1 loss and weaker NFE2L2 dependency first, then H7 MSI-high and stronger WRN dependency. In parallel, I registered lineage-interaction proposals for validated core effects and proliferation strata for H20 and H7 to assess heterogeneity and possible confounding by growth rate. These next steps should preserve the distinction between dataset-supported associations and external biological claims.

Current evidence is strongest for five dataset associations: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency and independently validated; PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency and independently validated; TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency and independently validated; MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency and robust but not independently validated; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency and robust but not independently validated. This iteration registers comparisons that either test whether the core accepted effects are stable under additional biological or technical contexts, or target remaining unresolved DNA-repair/RTK questions without promoting the KRAS co-mutation cluster. First, I add co-alteration strata that could strengthen or clarify accepted effects: PTEN loss within TP53-loss cells for STAT3, TP53 loss within KEAP1-loss cells for USP7, and KEAP1 loss within ARID1A-loss cells for NFE2L2. Second, I add high-screen-ROC strata for MSI-high/WRN and KEAP1/NFE2L2 to test whether the large effects persist among higher-quality screens, and a high-ploidy stratum for SMARCA4 loss/SMARCA2 to test a copy-number-associated cell context. Third, I register direct histology subtype contrasts for SMARCA2 and WRN, because lineage subtype is still an untested direct predictor for these outcomes even though lineage-specific exposure effects are under study. Fourth, I add targeted refinements for unresolved DNA-repair and RTK/MAPK questions: BRCA2-loss effect among adenocarcinoma cells for DHX9, RB1-loss effect among squamous cells for KIF18A, EGFR amplification among KRAS-wildtype and PIK3CA-wildtype cells for EGFR dependency, and NF1 loss for RIT1 dependency as a broad MAPK-pathway probe. I set core co-alteration and QC strata in the accepted direction where stability is expected, while setting exploratory histology, DNA-repair, RTK, and MAPK probes as uncertain. If the KEAP1/NFE2L2 and MSI/WRN strata remain stable, the next appraise stage should prioritize independent validation of KEAP1 loss/weaker NFE2L2 dependency or MSI-high/stronger WRN dependency. All conclusions remain observational associations in this supplied lung-cell-line dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

This analysis batch is centered on the core dataset-supported dependencies and their stability across biological and screen-quality contexts, while adding one broad MAPK-pathway probe. For the two central accepted but not independently validated associations, I prioritize proliferation and screen-quality strata: H119 and H124 test KEAP1 loss against NFE2L2 dependency in high-growth and high-screen-ROC contexts, respectively; H120 and H125 test MSI-high against WRN dependency in the same contexts. These strata directly assess whether the enormous accepted effects remain clinically meaningful under more stringent biological or technical subsets. For validated core effects, H116-H118 formally test whether the associations vary by lineage subtype: SMARCA4 loss with SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss with USP7 dependency, and PTEN loss with STAT3 dependency. These are not intended to change the accepted effects unless the interaction is large and decisive, but they are informative for biological or technical heterogeneity. I also test plausible co-alteration contexts that could affect interpretation of accepted effects: H121 tests PTEN loss within TP53-loss cells for STAT3, H122 tests TP53 loss within KEAP1-loss cells for USP7, and H123 tests KEAP1 loss within ARID1A-loss cells for NFE2L2. H126 tests SMARCA4 loss within high-ploidy cells, a copy-number/aneuploidy context relevant to SMARCA2 dependency. Finally, H130 probes NF1 loss with RIT1 dependency as a broad MAPK-pathway comparison. I am not prioritizing further KRAS co-mutation or EGFR conditional claims now, because prior KRAS refinements failed or remained imprecise and EGFR overall is unresolved after validation. Results should be judged relative to approximate 10% relative thresholds: for most dependency scores near -0.25 this is roughly 0.025-0.03 mean-score shift, while the accepted SMARCA2, WRN, NFE2L2, USP7, and STAT3 effects are far larger. Stable large positive signed estimates in core strata will support later independent validation of H20 and H7; modest, null, or highly imprecise results will be treated as context-specific or inconclusive observational evidence only.

This batch strongly reinforces the core dataset associations and gives little support to the new MAPK-pathway or formal lineage-heterogeneity claims. The estimates are already signed to the hypothesis direction, so positive values support the claimed association. H119 shows that KEAP1 loss remains associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency among high-growth-rate cells: signed estimate +0.835, 95% CI +0.793 to +0.879, exposed n=78. This is enormous relative to the approximate 10% relative threshold for dependency_NFE2L2 and excludes the null, so I accept and close this stratum. H120 similarly shows that MSI-high remains associated with much stronger WRN dependency among high-growth-rate cells: +0.785, CI +0.722 to +0.847, exposed n=35. Despite the smaller exposed cell, the estimate is extremely far above the approximate threshold for WRN dependency and excludes null; accepted and closed. H124 and H125 provide screen-quality robustness: MSI-high/WRN +0.790, CI +0.751 to +0.829; KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2 +0.793, CI +0.764 to +0.822. Both are accepted and closed. The co-alteration strata also support the accepted core effects rather than overturning them: H121 PTEN loss within TP53-loss cells for STAT3 is +0.190, CI +0.085 to +0.296; H122 TP53 loss within KEAP1-loss cells for USP7 is +0.493, CI +0.351 to +0.635; H123 KEAP1 loss within ARID1A-loss cells for NFE2L2 is +0.776, CI +0.730 to +0.823; H126 SMARCA4 loss within high-ploidy cells for SMARCA2 is +0.772, CI +0.745 to +0.799. These are far above outcome-specific clinical thresholds and are accepted and closed as robustness strata. Formal lineage interactions were not decisive. H116 rejects the claimed adenocarcinoma-specific enhancement of the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2-dependency association: signed interaction -0.028, CI -0.076 to +0.020, with the positive upper bound below the approximate SMARCA2 threshold. H117 and H118 remain inconclusive for USP7 and STAT3 lineage heterogeneity: intervals are wide and include null, so I leave them unresolved and closed. H130 rejects the NF1-loss/stronger RIT1-dependency probe: signed estimate -0.021, CI -0.049 to +0.008, point in the opposite direction and upper bound below the approximate RIT1 threshold. Because H20 KEAP1 loss/weaker NFE2L2 dependency is now accepted across many strata but has not yet had independent validation, I request validation of H20. All conclusions remain observational associations in this supplied lung-cell-line dataset, not causal or generalizable biological claims.

This synthesis is the final scientific report for the current evidence in the supplied dataset.

New validation: H20 is independently validated and closed. KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Discovery R8 signed estimate +0.796 (95% CI +0.776 to +0.816); independent validation R79 signed estimate +0.829 (independent CI +0.800 to +0.857). Both intervals exclude zero even at stricter validation alpha and are far above any ~10% relative difference threshold for NFE2L2 dependency. Because more negative scores mean stronger dependency, positive signed estimates mean KEAP1-loss cells have higher/less negative NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker dependency. This corroborates rejection of the original opposite-direction H8 claim.

Response deadline H96: the KRAS mutation effect in STK11-loss, TP53-wildtype cells had discovery R50 +0.052 (CI +0.008 to +0.096), but validation R53 +0.017 (independent CI -0.058 to +0.092). The validation point is below the approximate 10% relative threshold and does not reproduce the discovery effect, although the interval remains compatible with a clinically meaningful effect. I leave H96 unresolved and closed rather than reject, but this KRAS co-mutation refinement is not accepted and should not be promoted.

New validation H69: BRAF V600E versus RIT1 dependency is null/uncertain. Discovery R35 +0.004 (CI -0.025 to +0.033) and validation R80 -0.002 (independent CI -0.043 to +0.039). Both are imprecise, though validation includes clinically meaningful positive values; leave unresolved and closed with no further follow-up.

Current supported findings: independently validated dataset associations are H5 SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, H17 PTEN loss with stronger STAT3 dependency, H73 TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, and H20 KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. H7 MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency remains accepted on discovery and many robustness strata but is still the main core association not independently validated. All are observational associations among 2000 lung-cell-line profiles, not causal mechanisms or externally generalizable claims.

Negative or unsupported results remain informative: BRAF V600E did not support stronger BRAF dependency; ERBB2 amplification did not support overall ERBB2 dependency or adenocarcinoma-specific enhancement; ARID1A loss did not support SMARCA2 dependency; MYC amplification did not support POLR2A or USP7 dependencies; overall EGFR amplification failed to validate as a clinically meaningful effect; overall KRAS dependency was not decisive; lineage heterogeneity for SMARCA4/SMARCA2 was not supported; NF1 loss did not support RIT1 dependency; TP53 loss did not support stronger DHX9 dependency in the original direction.

Unresolved questions include conditional EGFR effects, KRAS co-mutation contexts after failed validation, formal lineage heterogeneity for USP7 and STAT3, research-marker/TMED10 signals, MYC-related RPL11 and KIF18A, TP53-MDM2 contexts, and BRCA2-related DHX9/WRN effects.

Most informative next analysis: request independent validation of H7 MSI-high and stronger WRN dependency. If it validates, close the core MSI/WRN claim; if it fails, reassess H7 as a discovery-only robust-stratum association. Otherwise, remaining analyses are lower priority explorations.
